claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy has a single-phase microstructure.
The initial high-entropy alloy is currently used as an intermediate plasma-facing component.
The initial alloy has moderate heat-transfer performance.
A controlled sub-micrometer dispersion of WC nanoparticles can be introduced into the high-entropy alloy during processing.
Dispersed WC nanoparticles create additional continuous thermal-conduction paths in the alloy.
Dispersed WC nanoparticles act as obstacles to dislocation movement.
WC nanoparticles have higher intrinsic thermal conductivity than the high-entropy alloy matrix.
WC nanoparticles form conductive networks that improve overall heat dissipation.
The WC dispersion impedes microstructural coarsening during thermal cycling.
Inhibiting dislocation propagation and microstructural coarsening maintains the mechanical strength of the alloy.
The WC nanoparticle intervention will increase heat-transfer capability by roughly 20% relative to current intermediate-layer alloys.
The WC nanoparticle intervention will cause no significant compromise in yield strength.
The WC nanoparticle intervention will cause no significant compromise in fracture toughness.
The predicted thermal and mechanical benefits will hold at 500–700°C under cyclic mechanical loading representative of intermediate plasma-facing layers.
Current intermediate-layer materials without WC nanoparticles degrade in performance during prolonged high-temperature cycling.
Excessive WC content or an inhomogeneous WC distribution can cause brittleness or degraded mechanical performance.
Operation substantially outside 500–700°C may prevent the predicted benefits.
Unexpected irradiation-damage modes may prevent the predicted benefits.
